claims.evidence: Darwin's examples of instinct variation are migration (extent, direction, total loss) and nest form; this test addresses the migration example only. 'Varies within species in a state of nature' is operationalised as partial migration: a species whose populations or individuals differ in whether or how far they migrate. AVONET's Migration score (1 sedentary, 2 partially migratory, 3 migratory) is an expert synthesis from handbooks; it is used for the global prevalence P. The GBIF index W checks that this classification corresponds to an observable pattern: a species whose individuals all migrate should have few winter records at breeding latitudes, whereas a partial migrant retains many. Recent records (2000 onward) are used because eBird dominates GBIF bird data and gives dense year-round coverage; the Northern Hemisphere restriction avoids mixing austral seasons. Latitude bands are global in longitude, so for species occurring on more than one continent (Sturnus vulgaris, introduced in North America) the index pools populations. Thresholds: 20 % of all bird species being partial migrants is taken as 'common'; 5 % as 'rare'. Direction of migration and the evolutionary loss of migration are not measured separately, since occurrence data cannot attribute a wintering bird to its breeding population. Registered measurement: 0.1089 (n=10986).

'Embraced by descent with modification' is read as single origin on the genealogy: a paraphyletic class (one origin, nested classes 'lost' from it, e.g. Reptilia relative to Aves) counts as embraced, a polyphyletic class (several origins) does not. claims.evidence: A 'progenitor' is read as an independent root of descent, i.e. a clade on the tree of life containing only members of the kingdom in question; the number of such clades needed to cover the kingdom is the number of progenitors the kingdom requires. Because the 1859 kingdoms differ from modern ones (Darwin's contemporaries placed ciliates, amoebae, foraminifera and gregarines among animals, and fungi, diatoms and blue-green 'algae' among plants), the count is made both for the modern kingdoms and for the kingdoms as understood in 1859; the pre-registered assignment follows the standard mid-19th-century arrangement (von Siebold 1845 for Protozoa; the botanical placement of fungi and algae). Diatoms were disputed (Ehrenberg: animals; most botanists: plants) and are assigned to plants; Euglenozoa were 'Infusoria' and are assigned to animals. The test uses the Open Tree synthetic tree as the independent genealogy; it does not test whether Darwin's own lower guess ('probably all organic beings from one primordial form') is right. claims.title: Boys and girls share a growth-velocity curve differing mainly in phase
claims.area: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.summary: The curves of growth velocity in boys and girls are of very similar shape but differ in amplitude and especially in phase, the girl's adolescent acceleration beginning and ending earlier than the boy's.
claims.assumptions: In short, throughout all this period, it is a very _similar_ curve in the two sexes; but it has its notable differences, in amplitude and especially in _phase_.
claims.evidence: Thompson's 'acceleration-curve' (mean annual increments) is what is now called a velocity curve; his Fig. 5 is for weight, from Quetelet, and the sentence generalizes to growth. 'Phase' is read as the timing of takeoff, peak and end of the adolescent spurt; 'amplitude' as the velocity level (reported, not scored, since the claim only says it differs). Cross-sectional NHANES medians attenuate and widen each sex's spurt relative to longitudinal curves, but a timing difference between sexes survives this smoothing. Modern US children, not Quetelet's 1830s Belgians. Registered measurement: 2.0 (n=23551).

claims.title: All animals pass through the same phases of growth: slow start, early peak, slowdown
claims.area: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.summary: In long-lived and short-lived animals alike, growth begins slowly, reaches its maximum velocity early, and then slows down (with temporary accelerations) toward a point where it ceases.
claims.assumptions: Whether the animal be long-lived, as man or the elephant, or short-lived, like horse or dog, it passes through the same phases of growth. In all cases growth begins slowly; it attains a maximum velocity early in its course, and afterwards slows down (subject to temporary accelerations) towards a point where growth ceases altogether.

claims.title: Cold-blooded animals approach a maximal size only asymptotically
claims.area: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.summary: In cold-blooded animals such as fishes the slowing of growth is greatly protracted, so that size seems never to reach a maximum but only to approach a limit asymptotically.
claims.assumptions: But especially in the cold-blooded animals, such as fishes, the slowing-down period is very greatly protracted, and the size of the creature would seem never actually to reach, but only to approach asymptotically, to a maximal limit.
claims.evidence: Thompson's 'size never actually reaches, but only approaches asymptotically, a maximal limit' is read as a contrast between an asymptotic growth curve (increments decline toward zero but stay positive at every age reached) and determinate growth (a maximum reached at a finite age, with zero increments thereafter while the animals are alive). 'Size' is taken as body length, the quantity recorded in surveys. The test uses cross-sectional survey means of length at age rather than individual growth histories; this is a modern reinterpretation forced by the data (Thompson's own fish examples were also population means). Fitted asymptotic parameters are not themselves used as evidence of an asymptote, as one assessor warned; the evidence is the model comparison against an explicit reached-maximum alternative and the sign of the late-age increments. Registered measurement: 0.6363636363636364 (n=11 species, 33 late-age increments, 1111408 aged fish from 986385 CA rows).

claims.title: Adult size results from both the rate and the duration of growth
claims.area: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.summary: The size an animal finally attains results from both its rate and its duration of growth: some species are larger because they grow faster (rabbit versus guinea-pig), others because they grow for longer (man versus rabbit).
claims.assumptions: The size ultimately attained is a resultant of the rate, and of the duration, of growth. It is in the main true, as Minot has said, that the rabbit is bigger than the guinea-pig because he grows the faster; but that man is bigger than the rabbit because he goes on growing for a longer time.

claims.title: Human length growth peaks in velocity around the fifth month before birth
claims.area: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.summary: The human curve of growth in length has a point of inflection about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: before it growth velocity continually increases, and after it, though growth remains rapid, velocity falls away.
claims.assumptions: It will at once be seen that there is a “point of inflection” somewhere about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: up to that date growth proceeds with a continually increasing velocity; but after that date, though growth is still rapid, its velocity tends to fall away.
claims.evidence: Thompson plots 'length' of the human foetus (crown-heel body length from His and other nineteenth-century sources) against age in months and locates an inflection about month five. No modern public standard measures crown-heel length continuously across gestation: ultrasound gives crown-rump length to 14 weeks and skeletal lengths afterwards, and body length is measured directly only at birth. The test therefore brackets the velocity peak from two body-length measures of the same consortium's population: crown-rump length (first trimester) and crown-heel length of newborns by gestational age at birth (24-42 weeks). Gestational ages are menstrual weeks; Thompson's 'fifth month' is taken as roughly 17-22 menstrual weeks, so months 4-6 (14-24 weeks) is the window consistent with 'about the fifth month'. Velocities of the median curve are used because the published standards are smoothed centile tables, not individual-level data. The rOpenSci gigs package redistributes the INTERGROWTH-21st published tables and equations as machine-readable files; those files are used, with the primary publications cited. No data values were inspected before this pre-registration. Registered measurement: 14.0 (n=169).

claims.title: Variability of stature and weight tracks the rate of growth
claims.area: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.summary: The coefficient of variability of human stature and weight falls when the rate of growth diminishes and rises again during the adolescent acceleration, so that variability is a function of the rate of growth.
claims.assumptions: We see, in short, that the amount of _variability_ in stature or in weight is a function of the _rate of growth_ in these magnitudes, though we are not yet in a position to equate the terms precisely, one with another.
claims.evidence: Thompson's evidence was Bowditch's and Boas & Wissler's cross-sectional CVs of Boston schoolchildren, ages 5-18 (stature CV about 4.8% at 5, 4.4% at 9, 5.8% at 14, 3.7% at 18). Modern reference charts are smoothed cross-sectional distributions of the same kind, so the LMS S parameter (approximately the CV) by age is the direct analogue. 'Rate of growth' is read as the absolute velocity of the median (cm/yr, kg/yr), Thompson's own usage (his Fig. 4 is the curve of annual increments). The WHO 2007 reference (5-19 years, height-for-age, both sexes) is a secondary replication, and the CDC infant tables (length and weight for age, 0-36 months) a descriptive check of Pearson's statement that variability decreases from birth; neither enters the verdict. Known confound (assessors): the adolescent CV rise is produced largely by variation in the timing of the spurt rather than by the rate itself; this does not affect the empirical association tested here. Before this pre-registration a reachability probe fetched statage.csv and wtage.csv and printed their header and first two rows (age 24 and 24.5 months); nothing else was inspected. Registered measurement: 4 (n=204).

claims.title: Plaice weight-length coefficient peaks near the size of sexual maturity
claims.area: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.summary: In plaice the weight-length coefficient k = W/L^3 is not constant but rises to a maximum and then slowly declines with increasing size, the maximum falling near 30 cm, about the size at which sexual maturity begins.
claims.assumptions: we see that _k_ is by no means constant, but steadily increases to a maximum, and afterwards slowly declines with the increasing size of the fish
claims.evidence: Thompson's k is the Fulton condition factor computed by length class from mean weights of trawl-caught plaice 'in a particular locality and at a particular time'. Modern survey fish are weighed individually, so class means of individual k are used, which is equivalent for the purpose. 'Near 30 cm' is read as 25-35 cm; 'about the size at which sexual maturity begins' is read as within 5 cm of the length at 50% maturity in the same samples, since the onset of maturity is not sharply defined. North Sea plaice today mature at smaller sizes than in 1907, so criterion (3) tests the coupling to maturity rather than the fixed 30 cm figure, while (2) tests the figure itself. Registered measurement: 43 (n=11474).

claims.title: Seasonal cycle in fish weight at fixed length is caused by spawning
claims.area: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.summary: In plaice of fixed length, weight falls from about November to March or April and is restored between May or June and November, a periodic change caused wholly by spawning and the subsequent rebuilding of tissues and gonads, so that the spawning season can be determined from length and weight alone.
claims.assumptions: With unchanging length, the weight and therefore the bulk of the fish falls off from about November to March or April, and again between May or June and November the bulk and weight are gradually restored. The explanation is simple, and depends wholly on the process of spawning, and on the subsequent building up again of the tissues and the reproductive organs.
claims.evidence: Thompson's table is for 55-cm fish from the 1909 Plaice Report, month by month. DATRAS does not give monthly coverage of the North Sea (NS-IBTS samples only Q1 and Q3), so the test uses the within-quarter trends that Thompson's smoothed curve predicts (decline Jan->Mar of roughly 7% per month; rise Jul->Sep of roughly 3-4% per month) and the maturity-stage contrast that is the direct signature of his mechanism. The word 'wholly' is tested with immature fish as the control that the assessors proposed: immature plaice do not spawn, so under the claim they should not share the cycle. Feeding and temperature covary with season and would produce a cycle in immature fish too; that is exactly what would refute 'wholly'. Planned years 2015-2024 (10 years, Q1 and Q3). Maturity codes are mapped before the data are seen: immature = {1, 61, A, I}; maturing = {2, 62, B}; spawning = {3, 63, C}; spent = {4, 64, D}; resting/skipped = {5, 65, E}; other codes (-9, 66, 6, F) excluded; mature = maturing + spawning + spent + resting. Length: LngtCode '1' means LngtClass in cm; '.' or '0' means mm (divided by 10). Fish with |residual log10 K| > 0.3 from the length-class/sex means are dropped as recording errors (pre-registered cleaning). A single probe request (NS-IBTS 2019 Q1 CA, HTTP status and first record only, a herring) was made before this pre-registration to confirm that the web service is reachable; no plaice data were inspected. Registered measurement: 1.285 (n=17187).

claims.title: Arizona tree rings show a regular 150-year climate periodicity
claims.area: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.summary: Century-smoothed annual ring widths of Arizona yellow pines show that the climate of Arizona over the past 500 years fluctuated with a regular period of almost exactly 150 years, probably mainly in moisture rather than temperature.
claims.assumptions: from which we seem compelled to draw the direct conclusion that the climate of Arizona, during the last 500 years, has fluctuated with a regular periodicity of almost precisely 150 years.
claims.evidence: Thompson relayed Douglass's (1909, 1914) reading of century-smoothed Flagstaff pine ring widths as showing a ~150-yr climatic cycle. 'Regular period of almost exactly 150 years' is read as a spectral line in the 130-170-yr band that is significant against a red-noise background, together with smoothed maxima recurring at 150 +/- 25 yr. The moisture-versus-temperature attribution is not tested. Modern ITRDB chronologies are standardized indices (age trend removed) built from many trees, not the few raw series Douglass had; they are the best available record of the same trees' growth signal. A 521-yr window holds only ~3.5 cycles of 150 yr, so the spectral test is low-powered and is complemented by the smoothed-maxima test. Registered measurement: 75.4 (n=521).

claims.title: The biconcave red blood corpuscle is not a surface-tension equilibrium figure

claims.summary: The biconcave mammalian red blood corpuscle is not a surface of constant mean curvature and so cannot be a fluid drop in equilibrium under surface tension alone; some other force, possibly osmotic inequilibrium or fluid-crystal forces of its cholesterin-like constituents, must maintain its shape, which changes to a sphere in diluted blood.
claims.assumptions: Accordingly, from the point of view of surface tension alone, the blood-corpuscle is not a surface of equilibrium; or in other words, it is not a fluid drop suspended in another liquid.
claims.evidence: Thompson's argument is that a fluid drop held by surface tension alone must have constant mean curvature 1/r1 + 1/r2 everywhere, and the biconcave corpuscle does not. We test the geometric premise on measured cells: a closed surface whose upper face is concave at the centre and convex at the rim cannot have constant mean curvature. The thickness map from quantitative phase imaging is used with the standard mid-plane symmetry assumption. The second clause, that corpuscles become spherical in diluted blood, and the suggested osmotic or fluid-crystal causes are not tested here. Species of the donor blood is taken from the data source's description; scope is mammalian red cells. Registered measurement: 0.7317 (n=1148).

claims.assumptions: we see that what we call its normal appearance is just one of many intermediate phases of shrinkage, brought about by the abstraction of fluid from its interior as the result of an osmotic pressure greater outside than inside the cell

claims.title: Cell-wall secretion is adsorption of constituents at the surface

claims.title: Hexagons are regular only where cells are equal in size and forces uniform
claims.area: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.summary: Perfectly regular hexagonal cell patterns occur only where the cells are uniform in size and subject to uniform forces, as in the retinal pigment epithelium; where cell sizes vary (intestinal epithelium, parenchyma) or growth adds directional traction, the hexagons become irregular or elongated.
claims.assumptions: the cells, uniform in size, are flattened out to a uniform thickness by the fluid pressure acting radially; and their reaction on each other converts the flattened discs into regular hexagons.
claims.evidence: Thompson's statement is comparative across tissues: perfectly regular hexagons where cells are uniform (retinal pigment epithelium) and irregular polygons where cell sizes vary (intestinal epithelium, parenchyma). No public dataset gives comparable per-cell segmentations of all three tissues, so the test is run within the tissue he names as the regular case, using natural variation in cell-size uniformity between regions of the human RPE mosaic (different retinal eccentricities and individuals). 'Regular hexagons' is operationalized topologically as the fraction of six-sided cells and the spread of neighbour numbers; 'uniform in size' as the coefficient of variation of apical cell area within the same region. 'Uniform forces' is not measured; the RPE as a non-proliferating monolayer under hydrostatic pressure is Thompson's own example of uniform forces, so the test isolates the size-uniformity part of his claim. Before this pre-registration only the Dryad file listing, the dataset README and the TIFF header tags (image size, bit depth, compression) of one participant's files were inspected, to confirm the segmentation images are readable; no cell outlines or measurements were examined. Post hoc data-cleaning rule (needed once the images were seen): the corrected segmentations cover only part of each 184 x 184 px ROI, leaving one large unsegmented component around the segmented patch; components with area > 3x the median interior cell area were treated as unsegmented regions and cells adjacent to them were excluded because their neighbour counts are incomplete. Registered measurement: -0.71 (n=21).

claims.evidence: Thompson's claim has two parts: a geometric description of the cell (hexagonal prism, three rhombic basal facets meeting at the tetrahedral angle 109 deg 28 min) and a minimal-surface rationale. Only the geometric description is tested here; the minimal-surface statement is a theorem about the rhombic dodecahedron (and is in fact not the true minimum, as Toth 1964 showed), not an empirical matter. The test requires 3-D geometry of bee-built cell bases. The two Dryad datasets listed were identified as the only public comb datasets found on Dryad, Zenodo and figshare on 2026-10-31; their README files were read to determine whether they contain basal-facet geometry before any data were downloaded.

claims.title: Minimal bisecting walls cut the longest axis and alternate at right angles
claims.area: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.summary: For a rectangular cell to be divided equally by a partition of least area, the partition must cut across its longest axis, and in successive bisections each new partition must be at right angles to the one before.
claims.assumptions: From this we may draw the simple rule that, for a rectangular body or parallelopiped to be divided equally by means of a partition of minimal area, (1) the partition must cut across the longest axis of the figure; and (2) in the event of successive bisections, each partition must run at right angles to its immediate predecessor.
claims.evidence: Thompson derives the rule for an ideal rectangular parallelepiped bisected by a least-area plane: the plane is perpendicular to the longest edge, and successive bisections alternate at right angles. Real meristem cells are not rectangular, so 'longest axis' is the largest principal axis of the cell volume and the test is restricted to mothers that are measurably elongated (principal-axis ratio >= 1.2), where the axis is defined. Successive divisions are identified only where both walls are still flagged as recent in one snapshot, so Part 2 samples rapid successive divisions. Division orientation in the shoot apex is also influenced by tissue stress, which can mimic or mask the geometric rule; the test measures the outcome, not the cause. Registered measurement: 35.85 (n=22810).

claims.title: A new cell wall has the least area that can enclose the given volume (Errera)

claims.summary: The fundamental rule of cell division is that the incipient partition of a dividing cell takes the least possible area that can divide the given volume; Sachs’s rule of successive divisions at right angles is a subordinate case of this principle.
claims.assumptions: a much more important and fundamental rule, due not to Sachs but to Errera; that (3) the incipient partition-wall of a dividing cell tends to be such that its area is the least possible by which the given space-content can be enclosed.
claims.evidence: Errera's rule as Thompson states it: the incipient partition has the least area that can divide the given space-content. The 'given space-content' is the observed volume split of the two sisters, so asymmetric divisions are included. Real walls may be curved; the minimum is taken over planes, so a curved minimal wall can have q < 1, which still counts as consistent. Sisters are identified from the dataset's own detection of recently formed walls (its pipeline flags thin, recent walls), not from lineage tracking; mis-identified pairs work against the claim. Sachs's subordinate rule (right-angle alternation) is tested separately under thompson1917-ch08-01. The test is on one model plant tissue (Arabidopsis shoot apex), within the claim's scope 'dividing cells, especially plant cells'. Registered measurement: 0.062 (n=27249).

claims.summary: A sector-shaped (triangular) cell is likely to divide by an anticlinal wall only when its angle of arc lies between about 62½° and 90°; narrower, more tapering cells divide by a periclinal wall, which then has the smaller area.
claims.assumptions: We see from this, then, that what we have called an anticlinal partition, as _MP_, is only likely to occur in a triangular or prismatic cell whose angle of arc lies between 90° and 62½°. In all narrower or more tapering cells, the periclinal partition will be of less area, and will therefore be more and more likely to occur.

claims.title: Uniform growth of a disc makes its daughter cells divide at different times
claims.area: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.summary: Uniform, symmetrical growth of a flattened disc does not imply uniform growth of its cells: after a quadrant divides into triangular and quadrilateral halves, the triangular cell gains area faster and reaches division size first (at about 1.345 times the radius, against about 1.517 for the quadrilateral).
claims.assumptions: For it shews us that a uniform and symmetrical growth of the organism (symmetrical, that is to say, under the limitations of a plane surface, or plane section) by no means involves a uniform or symmetrical growth of the individual cells, but may, under certain conditions, actually lead to inequality among these

claims.summary: Successive minimal-area divisions of a disc soon leave only quadrilateral cells at the periphery, which divide radially, producing a superficial layer of parallel-sided cells (an epidermis) contrasting with the irregular cells beneath.
claims.assumptions: we shall consequently have a superficial or peripheral layer of quadrilateral cells, with sides approximately parallel, that is to say what we are accustomed to call _an epidermis_.

claims.assumptions: But it would appear that the most stable arrangements are those in which the total number of contacts is most evenly divided, and the least stable are those in which some one cell has, as in type _f_, a predominant number of contacts.

claims.title: Division plane depends on the ratio of growth rate to division frequency
claims.area: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.summary: A growing cell divides according to the shape it has reached, set by the ratio of its growth rate to its division frequency: if markedly oblong it divides transversely, if a little more than a hemisphere obliquely, and if less than a hemisphere by a vertical wall along its axis.
claims.assumptions: the manner in which this latter cell divides will simply depend upon the form it has assumed before each successive act of division takes place, that is to say upon the ratio between its rate of growth and the frequency of its successive divisions.

claims.summary: The form of a growing organism regulates the form and number of the cells that compose it: the cell network is the result, not the cause, of the overall configuration, which is caused by whatever processes make growth faster in one direction than another.

claims.summary: Calcareous and other skeletal deposits are, as a rule, precipitated not within actively living protoplasm but in dead or inactive formed material, such as the intercellular matrix or the cell-wall, so their form is not directly shaped by the living cells.

claims.title: Calcium salts precipitate when the albumins holding them in solution break down
claims.area: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.summary: Albumin increases the solubility of calcium carbonate and phosphate, whereas its breakdown products dissolve them much less; hence skeletal calcium salts are thrown down when proteins are broken down in metabolism, not by direct action of carbonic acid on a more soluble salt.
claims.assumptions: The probability is, therefore, that the actual precipitation of the calcium salts is not due to the direct action of carbonic acid, etc. on a more soluble salt (as was at one time believed); but to catabolic changes in the proteids of the organism, which tend to throw down the salts already formed, which had remained hitherto in albuminous solution.

claims.area: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.summary: Skeletal elements comparable in size to a single cell (sponge spicules, radiolarian and foraminiferal skeletons) are shaped by molecular forces such as surface tension, whereas massive skeletons such as vertebrate bones are shaped by gravity, muscle action and mechanical loads, so scale produces essential differences in their controlling forces and forms.

claims.assumptions: let us suppose that it is confined either within a cell-wall or in adhesion thereto; it at once follows that its line of growth will be simply a geodetic to the surface of the cell.

claims.title: Triradiate spicules form at three-cell junctions with rays at 120°, four-rayed at ~109°
claims.area: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.summary: Skeletal material deposited between cells or within their partitions takes the shape of the cell junctions: in a layer of equal cells, where partitions meet in threes at 120°, it forms triradiate spicules with rays at 120°, and in a solid aggregate of four cells it forms tetrahedral four-rayed spicules with rays at about 109°; unequal cells give unequal angles and curved rays.

claims.summary: On a right cone the spiral geodetic coils more and more closely as the cone narrows, and the sutural line and parallel striations of a turreted spiral shell such as Turritella are geodetics of this kind.

claims.title: Eggs are prolate spheroids, never oblate

claims.evidence: Thompson's 'prolate, never oblate spheroid' is read as: the axis of rotational symmetry (the pole-to-pole length, which in asymmetric eggs runs through the blunt and pointed ends) exceeds the equatorial diameter. Published egg measurements record length and breadth with length along the polar axis, so L/B >= 1 means prolate and L/B < 1 would mean oblate. A limitation stated up front: because measurers conventionally record the longer dimension as length, a truly oblate egg could only reveal itself in such data as L/B at or just below 1 (an apparently spherical egg); the test therefore asks whether any species approaches that boundary, and the fraction of near-spherical eggs is reported as the zone where the data cannot discriminate. claims.evidence: Thompson's 'expansion in one transverse dimension compensated by compression in the other' is read as negative covariation of depth and width at a given length among related fishes; 'related' is operationalized as the same family (FishBase family names used in FishShapes). claims.title: A rule-90-type cellular automaton produces a nested self-similar pattern
claims.area: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.summary: A one-dimensional cellular automaton in which each cell becomes black when exactly one of its two neighbors was black (rule 90), started from a single black cell, produces an intricate but regular nested pattern made of triangular pieces that are smaller copies of the whole.

claims.evidence: 'Nested triangular pieces that all have exactly the same form' is operationalised as exact self-similarity under doubling: the pattern of the first 2^k steps is three translated copies of the pattern of the first 2^(k-1) steps separated by an empty (white) inverted triangle; iterated down to k = 1 this means every triangular piece is a scaled copy of the whole. The rule is the Wolfram rule 90 (new colour = XOR of the two neighbours), started from one black cell on an otherwise white infinite line, which is simulated exactly on a line wide enough that boundaries never matter. As an independent external check the rows are compared with OEIS A001317 (Sierpinski's triangle rows read as binary numbers), which is tabulated independently of any cellular-automaton code. Registered measurement: 0 (n=11180714).

claims.title: Rule 30 from a single black cell produces an irregular, complex pattern
claims.area: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.summary: The elementary cellular automaton rule 30, started from a single black cell, produces a highly irregular and complex pattern with almost no overall regularity, rather than a uniform, repetitive or nested one.
claims.assumptions: Rather than getting a simple regular pattern as we might expect, the cellular automaton instead produces a pattern that seems extremely irregular and complex.
claims.evidence: Wolfram contrasts rule 30 with the three kinds of simple behavior he has just shown (uniform, repetitive, nested), so 'irregular and complex with almost no overall regularity' is operationalized as the failure of a quantitative detector for each simple kind plus near-incompressibility, measured on the interior of the pattern. The interior window deliberately excludes the left and right edges, where Wolfram himself notes (p. 27) some regularity (the periodic right edge and diagonal stripes on the left); the claim is about the overall pattern, and the edges are a vanishing fraction of the light cone. Detectors are finite: A_rep only checks space-time periods up to 64 steps, A_nest only scale factors 2 and 3, and compressors only the regularities they model, so a pass is bounded non-detection, not a proof of irregularity. Registered measurement: {'black_fraction': 0.5005, 'A_rep': 0.6247, 'A_nest': 0.5017, 'lzma_norm': 0.8816, 'bz2_norm': 0.9022} (n=4196352).

claims.title: Rule 110 from one black cell becomes periodic with period 240 after about 2780 steps
claims.area: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.summary: Rule 110 started from a single black cell resolves after about 2780 steps: one localized structure survives and interacts with periodic stripes from the left to give behavior that repeats every 240 steps.

claims.evidence: Rule 110 is the Wolfram rule number 110 (rule bit k = new colour for neighbourhood 4*left + 2*centre + right). From a single black cell at x = 0 the pattern occupies only x in [-t, 0] at step t (cells right of the origin stay white), so the natural fixed frame is the one in which the right edge is at rest; Wolfram's figures on pp. 32-39 are drawn in that frame. 'Behavior that repeats every 240 steps' is read as exact time-periodicity of the whole pattern inside the light cone of time t (the cells to the left of -t at time t+P are newly created stripes and are not compared). 'The outcome is finally clear after about 2780 steps' is read as the onset of this exact periodicity, with a 10% tolerance because the text says 'about'. 'One structure survives' is not quantified separately; it is covered by the periodicity of the whole interior. Registered measurement: 213 (n=8000).

'Fixed size' includes patterns that die out (rules 0, 128), that flash with the background (7, 127) and that move at constant speed without changing width (2, 103). 'Grow forever' is operationalised as a width that keeps increasing between the third and fourth quarters of the run, which also captures the square-root growth of rule 225 noted in the text (width about 2*sqrt(t)). 'More complicated than repetition' is the complement of space-time periodicity with small period and drift inside the light cone, which is how a purely repetitive growing pattern (rules 50, 109) differs from a nested (22, 60, 90, 225) or random (30, 45) or complex (110) one. claims.title: No basic mobile automaton shows behavior beyond repetition or nesting
claims.area: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.summary: None of the 65,536 two-color mobile automata whose rule updates only the active cell shows behavior more complex than repetition or nesting; complex behavior appears only when the rule can also update the active cell's neighbors, and even then it is rare.
claims.assumptions: Of the 65,536 possible mobile automata with rules of the kind discussed so far it turns out that not a single one shows more complex behavior.
claims.evidence: 'Behaviour more complex than repetition or nesting' is operationalised by lossless compressibility of the step sequence, which is a complete description of the evolution from the fixed initial condition: periodic sequences compress to a constant, nested (substitution-generated) sequences compress to a slowly growing size, and sequences that are random-like or have irregular localised structures compress poorly. The threshold is fixed by calibration on classical reference sequences, not on the mobile automata themselves. Wolfram's own 'compressed form' (tape shown only when the active cell reaches a new extreme) is replaced by this generic measure. The rule convention is NKS p. 71: the rule reads (left, active, right) and writes the active cell's new colour and a direction; the extended rules (p. 73) also write both neighbours. The initial condition is all white with one active cell. Everything is generated by analysis.py; there is no external download. Registered measurement: {'basic_rules_complex': 0, 'basic_rules_nonperiodic_2000_steps': 218, 'extended_sample_complex_fraction': 0.0} (n={'basic_rules': 65536, 'extended_sample': 100000}).
claims.provenance: A New Kind of Science (2002). Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.assumptions: complex behavior almost never occurs except when large numbers of cells are active at the same time.

claims.title: Two- and three-state two-color Turing machines give only repetition or nesting
claims.area: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.summary: All 4096 two-state, two-color Turing machines, and all of the roughly three million three-state, two-color Turing machines started on a blank tape, ultimately produce only repetitive or nested patterns.
claims.assumptions: all ultimately turn out to yield just repetitive or nested patterns—at least if they are started with all cells white.
claims.evidence: 'Repetitive or nested' is operationalised through the subword complexity of the machine's step-letter sequence, which determines the whole space-time diagram given the rule: eventually periodic diagrams give bounded complexity and nested (self-similar) diagrams give complexity growing at most linearly in the factor length, whereas random-looking diagrams of the kind the book shows for four-state machines (p. 80-81) give complexity close to the window size. 'Ultimately' is bounded by the run lengths (1000, 20000, 200000 steps) with transients discarded; a machine with a transient longer than 100000 steps would be misclassed, and that limit is stated. The enumeration uses the book's numbering scheme (NKS p. 888) and its conventions (p. 78): s states, 2 colours, rule entries (new state, new colour, move +-1), blank tape, head in state 1. Registered measurement: 0 (n=2990080).
claims.provenance: A New Kind of Science (2002). Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.title: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only produce nested patterns
claims.area: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.summary: Substitution systems in which each element is replaced according to its own color alone always produce nested patterns, so obtaining behavior more complicated than nesting requires rules that depend on at least one neighboring element.
claims.assumptions: To get behavior that is more complicated than simple nesting, it follows therefore that one must consider substitution systems whose rules depend not only on the color of a single element, but also on the color of at least one of its neighbors.
claims.evidence: Wolfram's 'nested pattern' is given a formal operational content as low (sub-exponential, at most polynomial) subword complexity, which is the standard combinatorial signature of self-similar/morphic sequences: the Thue-Morse, Fibonacci and Cantor examples he gives all have p(n) = O(n). Rules whose replacement for some colour is the empty string, or that keep every string bounded, are included in the enumeration but can only give finite or eventually periodic output, which is trivially nested; the complexity test is applied to growing runs only. The claim's second half ('more complicated behaviour requires neighbour dependence') is tested only in the direction that neighbour-dependent systems can exceed the complexity bound, as a check of discriminating power; the universal statement itself is tested by exhaustive enumeration of two finite families. Registered measurement: 231 (n=5109).
claims.provenance: A New Kind of Science (2002). Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.title: One-element-deletion tag systems reduce to neighbor-independent substitution
claims.area: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.summary: A tag system that removes only one element per step always acts as a slow version of a neighbor-independent substitution system and so produces only repetitive or nested patterns, whereas removing two elements per step can yield very complicated behavior.
claims.assumptions: if only one element is removed at each step, then a tag system always effectively acts just like a slow version of a neighbor-independent substitution system of the kind we discussed on page 83.
claims.evidence: Tag systems follow NKS p. 93-94 and the implementation note (p. 894): at each step n elements are removed from the front and a block determined by the removed n elements is appended; a sequence shorter than n becomes empty. 'Neighbor-independent substitution system' is the map replacing each symbol by its block (NKS p. 83). 'Repetitive or nested' is operationalized as finite state space (eventual periodicity) or linear factor complexity (p(10) <= 60 for a two-letter sequence; the Thue-Morse sequence has p(10) = 28). 'Very complicated' is operationalized as non-terminating, non-recurring evolution with a length series that lzma cannot compress much better than its own shuffle. The test is computational; the program family is generated by analysis.py. Registered measurement: 376 (n=50625).

claims.title: Simple cyclic tag systems show random fluctuations in sequence growth
claims.area: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.summary: Some cyclic tag systems with two alternating blocks, started from a single black element, produce sequences whose average growth is steady but whose fluctuations about that growth are in many respects random.
claims.assumptions: if one looks at the fluctuations in this growth, as in the plots on the next page, then one finds that these fluctuations are in many respects random.
claims.evidence: Wolfram's 'fluctuations in this growth ... are in many respects random' (p. 95-96) is read as: fluctuations about the mean growth are unbounded and scale diffusively like a random walk (Hurst exponent near 1/2), and the binary sequence of leading elements, which fully determines the growth, cannot be compressed to a small fraction of its length (so it is neither periodic nor nested, in contrast to the book's example (c), whose leading column is a nested Sturmian sequence). 'Steady growth' is read as a linear fit with R^2 >= 0.999 and stable local rates. The family is the smallest natural family containing the book's examples (d) and (e). This is a computational test; no external data is needed. Registered measurement: 0 (n=225).
claims.provenance: A New Kind of Science (2002). Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.title: Axis crossings of Sin[x] + Sin[a x] follow a continued-fraction substitution system
claims.area: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.summary: For a sum of two sine functions Sin[x] + Sin[a x], the arrangement of axis crossings is generated by a generalized substitution system whose rule at each step comes from successive continued fraction terms of (a - 1)/(a + 1), giving nested patterns when a is a quadratic irrational.
claims.assumptions: for any curve like Sin[x] + Sin[α x] the relative arrangements of these crossing points turn out to be related to the output of a generalized substitution system in which the rule at each step is obtained from a term in the continued fraction representation of (α - 1)/(α + 1).
claims.evidence: Wolfram (p. 146) says the relative arrangement of the crossing points is 'related to' the output of a generalized substitution system whose rule at each step comes from a term of the continued fraction of (a-1)/(a+1), with repetitive (hence nested) structure when a is a square root. The two 'regularly spaced families' are the zeros of the two factors of sin x + sin ax = 2 sin((1+a)x/2) cos((1-a)x/2); their spacings are in ratio theta = (a-1)/(a+1), so the merged labelled sequence is a Sturmian (mechanical) word and the natural substitution system is the standard one driven by the partial quotients of theta (the word's own slope theta/(1+theta) has continued fraction [0; c_1+1, c_2, ...], so the directive sequence is exactly the partial quotients of theta). 'Related to' is operationalised as equality of factor languages, the strongest sense in which a finite segment of a mechanical word can match a substitution word whose intercept is not specified. The test uses exact arithmetic for the quadratic surds' continued fractions and double precision elsewhere, with partial quotients used only while the convergent denominators are below 10 N. Registered measurement: 31 (n=31).

'Randomness' is operationalised as incompressibility by a general-purpose compressor (lzma) plus block-frequency uniformity, following the assessors' remark that the claim locates randomness in the digit sequence. claims.evidence: Wolfram's 'local set of constraints' on a one-dimensional array of coloured cells (p. 210-211: each cell's neighbourhood must be one of a given set of allowed configurations) is a one-dimensional subshift of finite type: a set of allowed words of a fixed window length w over k colours. 'Can be satisfied at all' is read as the existence of a bi-infinite arrangement all of whose windows are allowed; by compactness this is equivalent to the existence of arbitrarily long valid finite words, and operationally it is tested by the existence of a valid word of length 4V + w (any valid word longer than V must revisit a de Bruijn vertex, so this length is far beyond the threshold, and the check is done by a reachability iteration, not a cycle search). 'Simple and purely repetitive arrangement' is read as a periodic configuration, found by brute-force enumeration of all period words u with |u| <= V = k^(w-1) and checking all cyclic windows. All constraint systems are enumerated exhaustively for (k, w) in {(2,2), (2,3), (2,4), (3,2), (4,2)} and sampled with a fixed seed for (2,5) and (3,3). Registered measurement: 1.0 (n=129939).

claims.title: Finite discrete deterministic systems must eventually repeat
claims.area: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.summary: Any system of limited size made of discrete elements and following definite rules must eventually exhibit repetitive behavior, with repetition period at most equal to its total number of possible states.
claims.assumptions: it is then a general result that any system of limited size that involves discrete elements and follows definite rules must always eventually exhibit repetitive behavior.
claims.evidence: Wolfram's 'system of limited size that involves discrete elements and follows definite rules' is read as a deterministic map f on a finite set of N global states, so 'definite rules' means the next state depends only on the current state. 'Eventually exhibit repetitive behavior' is read as: the orbit s, f(s), f(f(s)), ... is eventually periodic, with the eventual period (cycle length) at most N; the text's surrounding argument (p. 255) gives exactly this bound. Three concrete families of finite systems from the book's own repertoire are enumerated: the 256 elementary cellular automata on cyclic rings of n cells (N = 2^n), the 4096 two-state two-color Turing machines on cyclic tapes of n cells (N = 2 * n * 2^n: head state x head position x tape contents), and the modular multiplication maps x -> m x mod n (N = n). For every system every state is used as an initial condition, so the test is exhaustive within the enumerated sizes. The claim is a theorem (pigeonhole principle); the computation checks that the stated bound is never exceeded in these families and records how close observed periods come to it. Registered measurement: 1.0 (n=6896875).
claims.provenance: A New Kind of Science (2002). Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.title: Repetition periods of class 3 rules grow rapidly with system size
claims.area: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.summary: In cellular automata on a finite cyclic lattice, a rapid increase of repetition period with lattice size is characteristic of class 3 behavior, with large fluctuations as size changes; among elementary rules only rule 45 appears to give periods always near the maximum possible.
claims.assumptions: In general, a rapid increase with size is characteristic of class 3 behavior. Of the elementary rules, however, only rule 45 seems to yield periods that always stay close to the maximum of 2^n.

claims.title: Class 3 randomness can arise without randomness in initial conditions
claims.area: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.summary: The randomness of class 3 systems is not merely inherited from random initial conditions: random behavior can be generated even when the initial conditions contain no randomness at all.
claims.assumptions: the crucial point that I discovered only some time later is that random behavior can also occur even when there is no randomness in initial conditions.
claims.evidence: 'Random behaviour' is read as the book itself reads it (practical randomness, pp. 261 and 1085 ff.): the sequence passes standard statistical tests and is incompressible, not algorithmic randomness, which no finite test can establish. 'No randomness in initial conditions' is realised by the single-black-cell seed; the book's own comparison (p. 261) is with random initial conditions, so S2 is the matched control and S4 is a control for a deterministic but nested (non-random) sequence that the battery must reject for the test to be discriminating. Rule 22 is also mentioned in the claim's context but its single-cell pattern is nested; only rule 30, the book's example on this page, is tested. Registered measurement: 10 (n=1048576).
claims.provenance: A New Kind of Science (2002). Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.title: Additive rule 90 only transmits randomness from its initial conditions
claims.area: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.summary: Because rule 90 is additive, its patterns are superpositions of the single-cell nested pattern, so it cannot generate randomness intrinsically; any randomness it shows comes from the initial conditions, and deviations such as a low initial density persist forever, unlike in rule 22.
claims.assumptions: In rule 22 the low initial density has no long-term effect. But in rule 90 its effect continues forever.
claims.evidence: The claim has an algebraic clause (additivity, superposition) and an empirical clause (density persistence in rule 90 versus rule 22, the quoted sentence on p. 265). Additivity is checked exhaustively on the local rule and by exact superposition on random configurations. 'Cannot generate randomness intrinsically' is operationalized by the exact nested structure of the single-cell pattern plus the superposition identity: everything in a rule-90 pattern is a XOR of shifted copies of that nested pattern. 'Low initial density persists forever' is operationalized by the density at times 2^k, where rule 90 reduces to x_t(i) = x_0(i-2^k) XOR x_0(i+2^k) and the density must equal 2p(1-p) at arbitrarily late times; 'no long-term effect' in rule 22 is operationalized as late-time density independent of the initial density. Random initial conditions are Bernoulli(p) with fixed seeds; the lattice is a finite array measured only in a window unaffected by the boundaries within the run length. Rule numbering is Wolfram's standard code (rule 90 = l XOR r; rule 22 = exactly one of l, c, r black). Registered measurement: 0.00307 (n=33).
claims.provenance: A New Kind of Science (2002). Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.assumptions: By intrinsically generating randomness such systems in a sense have a certain fundamental stability: for whatever is done to their initial conditions, they still give the same overall random behavior, with the same large-scale properties.

claims.title: Spatially periodic initial conditions always give repetitive behavior
claims.area: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.summary: In any cellular automaton, an initial condition consisting of a fixed block of n cells repeated forever leads to repetitive behavior with period at most 2^n, since each block evolves like a finite cyclic system.
claims.assumptions: in any cellular automaton it is inevitable that initial conditions which consist just of a fixed block of cells repeated forever will lead to simple repetitive behavior.
claims.evidence: 'Initial conditions which consist just of a fixed block of cells repeated forever' is a spatially n-periodic configuration on the infinite line. 'Simple repetitive behavior' is read as eventual time-periodicity of the configuration, and the stated bound 2^n is read, following Wolfram's own reasoning and the assessors, as k^n for k colours (2^n in the two-colour case the text has in mind). 'Any cellular automaton' cannot be enumerated, so three families are tested: all 256 elementary rules exhaustively (n = 1..12), all 2187 three-colour nearest-neighbour totalistic rules (n = 1..6, bound 3^n), and a fixed-seed random sample of 500 two-colour range-2 (5-neighbour) rules out of 2^32 (n = 1..10). The reduction 'each block evolves like a finite cyclic system' is tested separately by simulating the actual repeated-block line and comparing it with the ring. Registered measurement: 1.0 (n=5507844).
claims.provenance: A New Kind of Science (2002). Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.title: Additive rules self-emulate; rules 90 and 150 are the only elementary ones
claims.area: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.summary: Every additive cellular automaton rule can emulate itself and therefore yields nested patterns, and among two-color nearest-neighbor rules the only fundamentally different additive rules are rules 90 and 150; self-emulation is otherwise rare, though non-additive examples such as rule 184 exist.

claims.evidence: 'Additive' is read as linear over GF(2) (Wolfram's own definition on p. 264: patterns from two initial conditions can be superimposed by XOR). 'Emulate itself' is read as block emulation with 2 to 4 cells per block and 1 to 4 steps per emulated step. 'Fundamentally different' is read as 'not related by left-right reflection and not related by the sublattice/shear relation that maps the rule 60 pattern onto the even sublattice of the rule 90 pattern'; without the second identification rule 60 (and its mirror 102) would be a third additive rule, which the test records explicitly. 'Rather rare' is given the threshold 25 % of the non-additive rules. All patterns are generated by analysis.py; there is no external download. The lattice is analysed on the full state recurrence; generators that output only high-order bits (ANSI C, drand48) are analysed on the state, which is the sequence whose stripes Wolfram's pictures show. claims.title: Non-overlapping replacement rules give update-order-independent causal networks

claims.evidence: Wolfram's generalized substitution systems (NKS pp. 497-503) replace one occurrence of a left-hand block at a time; which occurrence, and when, is the free choice of 'order'. A causal network has one node per replacement event and an edge from event P to event E whenever E's matched block contains an element that P produced; the initial condition is represented by a node 0 that 'produces' the initial elements. Two orders give 'the same causal network' if the networks are isomorphic as node-labelled directed graphs (labels = rule applied, node 0 fixed). Non-overlap is the syntactic condition of p. 503: no non-empty proper suffix of any block equals a prefix of any block (including the block itself), and no block is a substring of another. To compare complete histories across orders, the enumeration is restricted to systems whose every rule strictly shortens the string (|rhs| < |lhs|), so every evolution terminates after finitely many events; all complete evolutions (all choices at every step) from every initial string of length <= 5 over {A, B} are generated exhaustively. Wolfram's weaker condition (no overlap among strings actually generated) is not tested. Registered measurement: 1.0 (n=186).

claims.title: A fixed universal cellular automaton can emulate any cellular automaton

claims.evidence: The claim has two parts: the fixed 19-colour rule emulates any two-colour cellular automaton of any range (the note gives the encoding with range r as a parameter), and, via the reduction of multi-colour rules to two-colour rules with larger range (NKS p. 656), any cellular automaton whatsoever. This test checks the first part directly for r = 1 (all 256 rules) and r = 2 (random rules); the colour reduction is a separate construction and is not tested here, so 'any number of colours' is covered only through the general-range mechanism, not through a run of a multi-colour target. 'Rules more complicated than its own' is read as rule tables with more entries than the universal rule's own 19^5-neighbourhood description can be said to have: range-2 two-colour rules have 32 independent entries, already outside what elementary rules can express. claims.title: Cellular automata can emulate nearly all other system types, even computers
claims.area: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.summary: Cellular automata can be set up to emulate almost every type of system considered in the book—mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, sequential substitution and tag systems, register machines, arithmetic systems, logic circuits and random-access memory—and in principle a practical computer in its entirety.
claims.assumptions: But what I will show in this section is that in fact this is not the case, and that in the end cellular automata can actually be made to emulate almost every single type of system that we have discussed in this book.
claims.evidence: The claim is existential ('cellular automata can be set up to emulate ...'). The strongest finite test is to take the constructions the book itself supplies, run them against independent direct simulations of each emulated system, and look for counterexamples. Sequential substitution systems, tag systems, the multiplication CA, the RAM emulation and 'a practical computer' are not tested (the first two constructions use symbolic cell states whose decoding is not specified; the last is schematic), so a pass covers five of the eight named system types. Calibration before this pre-registration, disclosed here: the book's own examples (mobile automaton {35,57}, the 3-state Turing machine of p. 78, the substitution system {1 -> 10, 0 -> 01}, the register machine program of p. 99 and eight hand-written logic expressions) were used to fix the decodings. In that calibration the published register-machine construction failed on 14 of 60 and then 26 of 150 random programs. Tracing showed the cause: when an increment instruction fires while the register's only remaining cell is a pending-decrement signal (colour m+1 with background to its left, i.e. register value 0 whose deletion is still in flight), the published rule {_, _, p} -> m+3 converts the signal into an increment signal (worth two cells) instead of one cell. The repair adds one rule per increment instruction, {0, m+1, p} -> m+2 for i[1] and {p, m+4, 0} -> m+5 for i[2], placed before the published rules; 150/150 calibration programs were then exact. The main run uses a fresh seed. Registered measurement: 5 (n=172804).

claims.title: Cellular automata cannot emulate substitution systems step for step
claims.area: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.summary: Unlike mobile automata or Turing machines, substitution systems cannot in general be emulated one step per cellular automaton step, because the number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor each step while a cellular automaton pattern can grow only by a fixed amount per step; progressively more cellular automaton steps are needed per substitution step.
claims.assumptions: That this must ultimately be the case one can see from the fact that the total number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor from one step to the next, while in a cellular automaton the size of a pattern can only ever increase by a fixed amount at each step.
claims.evidence: The claim is a counting argument. Its premise (fixed growth per CA step) is checked exhaustively over the elementary rules and on random larger-radius rules; the second premise (multiplicative growth of substitution systems) is checked over the complete family of two-colour systems with blocks of length 0-3 (NKS p. 82-83 convention: every element is replaced by the block for its colour; an empty block deletes the element); the conclusion is quantified as the minimal number of CA steps per substitution step under the only assumption that each element occupies at least one cell of the pattern (the encoding Wolfram's figures use; a compressed encoding would fall outside the claim's 'size of a pattern' reasoning). The clause 'unlike ... Turing machines' is checked by an explicit one-step-per-step construction (NKS p. 657). Computational; all programs generated by analysis.py. Registered measurement: 32 (n=178).
claims.provenance: A New Kind of Science (2002). Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.title: Neighbor-independent substitution systems cannot emulate cellular automata
claims.area: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.summary: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only generate repetitive or nested patterns, so they cannot emulate cellular automata such as rule 30, whereas neighbor-dependent substitution systems can emulate cellular automata straightforwardly.
claims.assumptions: For as we discussed on page 83, neighbor-independent substitution systems can generate only patterns that are either repetitive or nested—so they can never yield the more complicated patterns that are, for example, needed to emulate rule 30.
claims.evidence: 'Repetitive' is operationalised as eventually periodic (bounded subword complexity, Morse-Hedlund), 'nested' as a self-similar word, which for fixed points of morphisms has subword complexity O(n^2) at most (Pansiot); the threshold (n+1)^2 at n = 14 is therefore a generous upper bound for repetitive-or-nested and about a tenth of what a random-like binary sequence of this length shows. 'Cannot emulate rule 30' is tested within the enumerated family by the complexity gap (a word with p(14) <= 225 cannot contain the rule 30 row, whose own p(14) is measured); it is not a proof over all encodings. The neighbour-dependent half is tested exactly as the book describes it (rules 'always yielding just one cell and corresponding quite directly to cellular automata', p. 666). Registered measurement: 157 (n=1924).

The implication itself is not empirical; what can be checked computationally is its first premise for a concrete system type. We check it for Turing machines, the second family named in the claim, by implementing a uniform emulation construction (the sweeping-head scheme NKS describes for Turing machines emulating cellular automata, p. 665-666, written here from scratch rather than copied) and testing it exhaustively on the elementary rules and on random rules with more colours and larger neighbourhoods. The second premise (existence of a universal cellular automaton) is taken from the published proof that rule 110 is universal; it is not re-derived. The other families in the claim (mobile automata, substitution systems, tag and cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems, register machines) are not tested here, so a 'supports' verdict confirms the claim's structure for one family only. claims.title: Simple arithmetic systems based on remainders can be universal

claims.summary: A system that repeatedly takes a whole number, computes its remainder modulo a constant and applies an arithmetic operation chosen by that remainder can emulate a register machine, and is therefore universal; given how widespread universality is, arithmetic supporting it is unsurprising.
claims.assumptions: The picture below shows that such a system can be set up to emulate a register machine. And from the fact that register machines are universal it follows that so too are such arithmetic systems.
claims.evidence: Wolfram's 'system that takes a whole number, computes Mod[n, 30], and applies one of several arithmetic operations chosen by that remainder' is the family of generalised Collatz maps n -> (p*n + q)/s with the branch chosen by n mod M. The specific register machine of Wolfram's figure is not transcribed in the online text, so instead of checking his single example the test checks the general construction he describes (encoding n = i + L * 2^a * 3^b, modulus 6L; for L = 5 this is his modulus 30) on a random sample of register machines plus growth programs. Register-machine conventions follow NKS Chapter 3 (pp. 97-102): decrement of a zero register is a no-op that moves to the next instruction, and the program wraps around cyclically. claims.title: Class 1 and 2 cellular automata cannot be universal

claims.summary: Cellular automata that produce only uniform or repetitive patterns (class 1 and class 2) can never be universal, because they transmit information only over limited distances and so support only processes involving a limited number of cells.
claims.assumptions: In a sense the fundamental reason for this—as we discussed on page 252—is that such class 1 and class 2 cellular automata never allow any transmission of information except over limited distances.
claims.evidence: The claim has a conclusion (class 1 and 2 automata cannot be universal) and a stated mechanism ('never allow any transmission of information except over limited distances'). Non-universality is a statement about all possible encodings and is not testable by finite computation; the test addresses the mechanism, which is the premise of Wolfram's argument: perturbations of class 1/2 states stay localized. Wolfram's classes are phenomenological, so they are operationalised here as 'settles into a temporal cycle of period <= 64 on an 800-cell ring within 1000 steps from random initial conditions'; the damage width (not displacement) is used so that shifting class-2 rules, whose perturbation moves but does not grow, count as bounded, as the assessors noted. Perturbations are applied to the settled state because the claim concerns the asymptotic behaviour, not transients. Registered measurement: 0.9792 (n=96).

claims.title: Nested-pattern and additive cellular automata cannot be universal
claims.area: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.summary: Cellular automata whose information transmission is highly constrained so that patterns are essentially nested, and additive rules such as rules 90 and 150 whose states after a power-of-two number of steps are simple superpositions of shifted copies of the initial condition, cannot be universal.
claims.assumptions: And since there are many kinds of behavior that do not return to such predictable forms after any limited number of steps, one must conclude that additive rules cannot be universal.
claims.evidence: The claim bundles a precise mathematical premise (power-of-two-step superposition for additive rules) with an informal class ('essentially nested' rules) and a non-universality conclusion. The test checks the premise exactly, checks that it discriminates additive rules from the complex rules the book contrasts them with, and cross-checks the nested single-cell patterns against externally tabulated sequences (Gould's sequence for rule 90, and the rule-150 analogue). It does not prove non-universality; a rule's universality depends on permitted encodings and no finite computation can exclude it, so 'supports' here means the premise and the discriminating contrast hold, not that the conclusion has been verified. claims.provenance: A New Kind of Science (2002). Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.title: Rule 54 shows only repetitive or nested forms in 100 million initial conditions
claims.area: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.summary: Rule 54, a possible class 4 elementary cellular automaton, shows only repetitive or nested behavior in its first hundred million initial conditions, leaving it uncertain whether rule 54 is universal.
claims.assumptions: And as one continues one sees various other repetitive and nested forms. But at least up to the hundred millionth initial condition one sees nothing that is fundamentally any more complicated.
claims.evidence: The claim is a finite observational statement about the first 10^8 initial conditions; the full census is beyond a few minutes of Python, so this is a scaled census (2^16 initial conditions) with the book's informal judgement 'nothing fundamentally more complicated than repetitive or nested' frozen into a local-complexity classifier. The classifier counts distinct 6 x 6 space-time tiles in the second half of the evolution: self-similar (nested) and periodic patterns have bounded tile vocabularies, whereas class 3 patterns have thousands and class 4 patterns with interacting gliders over a thousand. The threshold was set from controls outside the rule-54 family plus the book's own eight rule-54 examples; it is admittedly coarse, and the random-seed rule 150 controls (nested, up to 1007) show that nested patterns with wide seeds approach it. claims.title: Complete and consistent means exactly half of all strings are generated
claims.area: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.summary: For a multiway system serving as an axiom system, with negation any length-preserving involution on strings, the system is complete and consistent exactly when half of all possible strings of each length are eventually generated from the string representing true; more than half implies inconsistency and less than half implies incompleteness.
claims.assumptions: the criterion for whether a system is complete and consistent is simply that exactly half the possible strings of a given length are eventually generated if one starts from the string representing "true".
claims.evidence: The book (pp. 796-797) states the criterion as an equivalence ('the criterion for whether a system is complete and consistent is simply that exactly half ... are eventually generated') but argues only the two contrapositive directions. 'Negation' is taken as the book says: any operation that preserves length and gives back the original when applied twice (a length-preserving involution), including ones with fixed points (strings equal to their own negation), for which the test records separately what happens. 'Complete' = for every string, it or its negation is generated; 'consistent' = for no string are both generated (a fixed point that is generated counts as both). 'Eventually generated' is made exact by restricting to length-non-decreasing rules so that the generated set at each length is a finite closure. Registered measurement: 80 (n=14850).

claims.evidence: Wolfram's pictures (pp. 804-805) show, for a sequence of simple axiom systems, the operator forms (multiplication tables) allowed with 2, 3 and 4 elements, inequivalent under relabelling; his claim is that the vast majority of systems allow many forms and are 'not really about operators of any particular form', while a few (logic, i.e. Nand; junctional, equivalential and implicational calculi) force essentially a single form. This test reproduces that model enumeration for k = 2 and 3 only (k = 4 would require 4^16 tables per axiom, beyond the budget) over an explicit, exhaustively enumerated family of the simplest single-equation systems. 'Vast majority' is read as >= 80%, 'only a few' as <= 5%. Multi-axiom systems (e.g. group theory) are outside the enumerated family and are not needed for the majority statement. claims.title: Very short single-axiom systems for logic exist among the simplest axiom systems
claims.area: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.summary: Propositional logic can be axiomatized in terms of Nand by a single axiom with only six Nands (found by searching small axiom systems), far shorter than textbook systems, so an axiom system for logic is likely to be found among the simplest few thousand axiom systems.
claims.assumptions: So what this means is that if one were just to go through a list of the simplest few thousand axiom systems one would already be quite likely to find one that represents logic.
claims.evidence: Finite-model screening is a necessary condition for axiomatising Boolean algebra (every Boolean algebra is a model, and no 3-element algebra is), not a sufficient one; the sufficiency of the six-Nand axiom rests on the equational proof the book presents on pp. 810-811 (found with automated theorem provers) which standard tooling here cannot re-run. The test therefore checks everything about the claim that is checkable by enumeration: that the published axiom is consistent with being an axiom for logic on all domains up to 4 elements, that six Nands is the minimum passing even the weakest screens, and that a screen-passing system appears within the first few thousand systems of the book's own enumeration. 'Simplest few thousand' is read against the book's own ordering (by total number of Nands, systems {X = a} and {X = a, a.b = b.a}). Registered measurement: 100 (n=327042).

claims.title: Regeneration as descent to a free-energy attractor; induced shapes as local minima
claims.area: Emmons-Bell M 2015, Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms › 3. Discussion › 3.7. A hypothesis: Physiological Network Attractors Underlie Regions of Anatomical Morphospace
claims.summary: On the authors' proposed view, discrete planarian head patterns are the lowest free-energy outcomes of bioelectric network dynamics; amputation raises free energy and regeneration is a return to a low-energy attractor, octanol shifts the system to another attractor, and the induced other-species shapes are only local minima since worms return to the global minimum of G. dorotocephala morphology after about 3–4 weeks.

Only experimental evidence codes (EXP, IDA, IPI, IMP, IGI, IEP, HTP, HDA, HMP, HGI, HEP) are used, so electronic or sequence-similarity annotations cannot create the overlap. The universe is every gene with at least one such BP annotation, after removing NOT-qualified lines. 'Beyond the known shared ion channels, connexins and neurotransmitter machinery' is implemented by excluding from the universe every gene annotated (any evidence) to GO:0005216 ion channel activity, GO:0005243 gap junction channel activity, GO:0005921 gap junction, GO:0007268 chemical synaptic transmission, GO:0001505 regulation of neurotransmitter levels or GO:0030594 neurotransmitter receptor activity, with descendants. Only the first part of the claim is tested; its second part (memory genes appearing in cancer, regeneration and embryogenesis screens) is out of scope here. Registered measurement: 2.6573 (n=10243).

problems.known: The finite Price identity and a conditional Hamilton regression corollary have compiled. Total fitness variance is not generally additive genetic variance.
problems.next_action: Specify the genetic projection and partial-change operation against primary sources before any prover run.
problems.acceptance: Independent statement-fidelity review, exact target freeze, compiled projection/covariance correspondence, standard axiom audit and controls that distinguish total from additive variance.

problems.title: Determine what evidence could connect molecular predictions to tissue transport
problems.question: For one specified biological system, what measured and modeled quantities are needed to evaluate a transport claim?
problems.known: A protein structure prediction alone does not provide binding affinity, turnover or effective tissue diffusivity.
problems.next_action: Choose a matched assay and audit the measured quantities before proposing a BioNeMo computation.
problems.acceptance: A source-linked dataset with matching biological context, explicit transport/kinetic model, held-out calibration and a stated remaining uncertainty or documented insufficiency of evidence.

problems.title: Separate linear instability from the nonlinear pattern a simulation produces
problems.question: Within a frozen kinetics/domain/initial-condition ensemble, where do linear predictions and converged nonlinear outcomes differ?
problems.known: An admissible growing linear mode and a finite-time nonlinear pattern are different observables. Solver nonconvergence must remain visible.
problems.next_action: Align the existing runner's observables and convergence categories before interpreting its movies or aggregates.
problems.acceptance: Preregistered observables, amplitudes, horizons and tolerances; independent linear calculation; numerical convergence checks; unresolved cases reported; no universal biological threshold claim.

problems.title: Check that extracted claims preserve their source's actual meaning
problems.question: Which source-to-record mappings preserve the mathematical object, quantifiers, units and scope?
problems.known: The 21-record audit checks hashes and copied fields. It does not establish faithfulness to original papers. Several records already state conditions that a short headline hides.
problems.next_action: Begin with Fisher and Hamilton, then release independent source-review shards for the remaining records.
problems.acceptance: Pinned source and passages, reviewed mapping of statement/math/context, explicit disagreements and versioned corrections. Citation presence alone is insufficient.

problems.title: Demonstrate one independent, useful reuse across participants
problems.question: Can a second participant inspect and reuse a scoped contribution to change a different research action?
problems.known: Local self-tests and a coordination message do not demonstrate external reuse. Mycelium and other systems already provide close coordination precedents.
problems.next_action: Agree the Delphi contribution format and offer one small replay or source-review task to an existing participant.
problems.acceptance: Attributable second-participant run, exact consumed contribution version, applicability check, resulting artifact, independent review and measured overhead/cost.

problems.title: Test whether attention and resource allocation improve useful progress
problems.question: Which allocation rule improves accepted contributions or useful downstream decisions per constrained resource without starving exploration and replication?
problems.known: Votes, agent count and post volume do not establish scientific progress. Agent-economy proposals already discuss resource and credit allocation.
problems.next_action: Define the decision-maker's objective, acceptance predicates and resource constraints before choosing a voting or market mechanism.
problems.acceptance: Pinned task pool, separate interest/resource/blocking signals, preregistered utility and costs, expert-order and simple allocation baselines, coverage and failed/negative work included.

problems.title: Reject the volume-changing mode in the pinned liquid-bridge benchmark
problems.question: Which admissible perturbations preserve the declared bridge volume?
problems.known: The n=1 sine displacement has nonzero integral and violates the stated fixed-volume constraint; independent review caught the benchmark interpretation before its agent evaluation.
problems.next_action: Reuse this review as a regression check when future benchmarks define admissible modes.
problems.acceptance: Exact integral witness and primary-source correspondence under the stated fixed-volume interpretation, recorded in the linked review.

frontier.scope: Curated project questions drawn from existing reviews. These are not claims of newly discovered field-wide open problems.
